results.title: Uncertainty-Aware Joint Generative Modeling of Fault Event Sequences and Sensor Time Series in Solar PV Plants
results.snippet:
# Uncertainty-Aware Joint Generative Modeling of Fault Event Sequences and Sensor Time Series in Solar PV Plants
Hao Yan
###### Note to Practitioners
Photovoltaic (PV) plant operators face challenges in anticipating rare, multiclass faults from event logs alone. This paper introduces a multimodal generative model that combines sensor time-series data with fault event sequences to predict system behavior and future fault occurrences. The model employs generative decoders that provide probabilistic forecasts, enabling risk-sensitive maintenance planning. Practitioners can use the model to generate finite stochastic operating scenarios with a specified number of rollout iterations, forecast near-term fault timing and type, and inform proactive maintenance scheduling without interpreting the output as deterministic two-year extrapolation. The framework is demonstrated on data from the Red Rock Solar Site and can serve as a digital twin for evaluating maintenance policies safely via offline RL and off-policy evaluation before field trials. Key practical benefits include improved prediction for several low-frequency fault classes with sufficient historical support, uncertainty estimates for decision-making, and multiple plausible future scenarios for risk assessment; ultra-rare classes with only a few examples remain challenging and should be interpreted with their support counts.

In addition to forecasting, PV plants require robust condition monitoring to detect incipient failures and schedule maintenance. Recent surveys highlight the rapid adoption of AI for PV predictive maintenance, including anomaly detection, fault classification, and remaining useful life estimation from operational data [33, 34]. Distributed IoT and cloud-based frameworks have been proposed for predictive maintenance of solar panels [35]. Related work also covers PV layout and manufacturing inspection, wind-turbine fault diagnosis, and multisource fusion/prognostics [36, 37, 38, 2, 39, 40].

Our approach leverages these generative modeling advances to build a *joint* multi-modal simulator: a CLDM model generates multivariate sensor trajectories with quantified uncertainty, while a SMURF-THP decoder generates fault events with associated timing and type. Both decoders are conditioned on a shared cross-modal latent representation, explicitly capturing the coupled dynamics between PV system states and operational events. This unified design enables coherent scenario generation where sensor trajectories and fault occurrences are jointly sampled, supporting risk-aware maintenance planning through probabilistic forecasts of both continuous system behavior and discrete fault processes.

This work presented a multi-modal generative framework for the predictive maintenance of utility-scale photovoltaic systems. By integrating an iTransformer encoder for high-dimensional sensor streams and a Transformer Hawkes Process for discrete event histories via a co-attention mechanism, our model effectively captures the complex interplay between continuous operating regimes and sporadic fault occurrences.
A key contribution of this work is the hybrid decoder architecture: we replaced traditional deterministic forecasters with a *CLDM* for sensor trajectories and a *SMURF-THP* score-matching module for event timing. This design enables the generation of probabilistic, uncertainty-aware future scenarios rather than single-point estimates. Experimental evaluations on real-world data from the Red Rock Solar Site demonstrate that this approach not only achieves higher accuracy in fault prediction but also produces realistic, synchronized rollouts of sensor data and maintenance events.

results.title: The intention to adopt photovoltaic systems: integrating behavioral theories with mediation-moderation analysis
results.snippet:
This research aims to identify key areas where the intention to acquire photovoltaic systems might be improved. The purchasing intention of Photovoltaic systems is influenced by various individual theories, including the Theory of Planned Behavior, the Model of Technology Acceptance (TAM), and the Theory of the Diffusion of Innovations (DOI).

The present study introduces a comprehensive framework that aims to explain consumer interest in residential photovoltaics by incorporating aspects from Technology Acceptance Model, Theory of Planned Behavior, and Diffusion of Innovation. The study results demonstrate a robust and favorable impact of the Theory of Planned Behavior, the Technological Acceptance Model, and the Diffusion of Innovations on the intention to purchase photovoltaic systems. As anticipated by the DOI (Diffusion of Innovation) theory, the findings indicate that the innovativeness of DOI is positively associated with the inclination to engage in discussions about a potential purchase of a photovoltaic (PV) system. The results indicate that both the total effect and direct effect are statistically significant (S.E: 0.276, P: 0.000) accounting for 34 % of the overall contribution. Consumer novelty seeking had a significant beneficial impact on interest and also had favorable indirect impacts through perceived relative advantage. The TPB variables explained 31 % of the variance in interest, taking into account household limitations. The inclusion of social curiosity in the model revealed that the belief in the personal benefits of solar panels had the most powerful direct and overall impact on interest. This was demonstrated by the significant (S.E: 0.313, P: 0.000) direct and total effect on the intention to purchase a PV system for household use. The analytical findings demonstrate a direct and favorable relationship between the Technology Acceptance Model, also known as the TAM, and the intention to acquire photovoltaic (PV) systems in China.

results.title: Adaptive Residual Modeling for Scenario Learning in Probabilistic Load Forecasting
results.snippet:
Uncertainties in weather, user behavior, and distributed energy production introduce significant variability into feeder power. Effective power system operations require both multi-horizon load forecasts and well-calibrated extreme quantiles for the forecast. Nevertheless, standard objectives that fit the full forecast distribution often underemphasize rare observations and extremes. Conversely, applying heavy tail-weighting in the distribution to capture these extremes can distort the underlying probability distribution. To address this issue, this paper proposes adaptive residual modeling for scenario learning (ARMSL), a two-stage framework. Particularly, Stage I in our framework sequentially models environmental response, history-dependent load patterns, persistent residual deviations, and the remaining innovations. Upon the modeling, we then generate joint active- and reactive-power scenarios with state-dependent dispersion. Stage II keeps the scenario model fixed and calibrates extreme marginal quantiles using a simple, channel-specific reference forecast (an anchor). Only outward deviations from this anchor are admitted, with their contribution determined by local calibration history and the current operating state. From our numerical simulations on FeederBW dataset, Stage I outperforms diffusion baselines in energy and variogram scores. Our complete framework achieves an active-power 0.99-quantile pinball loss of 0.1932 (a 30.08% to 85.33% reduction relative to three baselines) with 1.054% exceedance rate against a nominal 1%. From simulations on the Rolle dataset, we observe decreased losses by 5.39%–14.40% compared to the active-power-only anchor. Furthermore, the unchanged Stage I scenarios in the simulation yield a correlation of 0.953 between predicted and observed feeder event rates, with 90.0% of feeder errors falling within two percentage points.

Probabilistic load forecasting typically employs quantile or Bayesian models to estimate marginal uncertainty, alongside scenario generators to simulate coherent joint trajectories [3, 4].

results.title: Harnessing artificial intelligence and machine learning for predictive maintenance and optimization in renewable energy systems: a mini-review
results.snippet:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) into renewable energy systems (RES) is increasingly recognized as a practical pathway for improving operational efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. Renewable sources, such as solar, wind, and hydropower, as well as hybrid configurations, are inherently intermittent and operationally complex, creating persistent challenges for grid stability, asset reliability, and energy optimization. Conventional maintenance strategies, whether reactive or preventive, often lead to unplanned downtime, inefficient inspections, and increased lifecycle costs. In response, AI/ML-enabled predictive maintenance (PdM) leverages high-frequency sensor data, SCADA streams, and historical performance records to detect anomalies, diagnose faults, and estimate remaining useful life (RUL), enabling proactive maintenance interventions. Beyond maintenance, AI/ML supports operational optimization through energy generation forecasting, load prediction, grid integration, storage scheduling, and adaptive control, thereby strengthening system resilience and lowering operational costs. Unlike prior reviews that treat PdM and RES optimization as separate topics, this work provides a unified, decision-oriented synthesis that explicitly links (i) maintenance outcomes (fault detection/diagnosis/RUL) and (ii) operational outcomes (forecasting, dispatch, storage scheduling, and grid control) through shared data pipelines and coupled decision trade-offs. The review further provides a structured mapping that connects AI/ML methods to (a) RES asset types (solar, wind, hydropower, hybrid, and emerging marine systems), (b) decision objectives (fault/RUL, forecasting, dispatch and control), and (c) deployment settings (IoT/SCADA, edge-cloud, and digital-twin-enabled monitoring). Emerging technologies, including digital twins, edge AI, federated learning, and explainable AI (XAI), are discussed as enabling mechanisms for real-time monitoring, privacy-preserving learning, adaptive decision-making, and transparency in critical infrastructure.

AI and ML have become foundational technologies for PdM in renewable energy contexts. They enable automated learning from SCADA streams, condition-monitoring signals (e.g., vibration, acoustic, thermal signatures), operational logs, and environmental variables to detect anomalies, diagnose faults, and forecast failure risk or remaining useful life (RUL) (; ). Advanced techniques such as deep learning models, ensemble learning, and representation learning have improved predictive accuracy in domains such as wind turbine drivetrain monitoring, photovoltaic fault classification, and hydropower component diagnostics (). The increasing integration of IoT devices further strengthens PdM capabilities by enabling continuous monitoring and high-resolution data acquisition across distributed RES assets (; ). Beyond maintenance, AI/ML also plays a critical role in operational optimization and grid integration of renewable energy. Accurate energy forecasting (solar irradiance, wind speed, and generation output) supports dispatch planning, reserve allocation, and market participation.

Machine Learning (ML) algorithms have become integral to modelling and optimizing renewable energy systems owing to their ability to handle complex, nonlinear, and high-dimensional data (). Three foundational families are most widely deployed in RES contexts.
Random Forests (RF): Ensemble learning methods such as RF are utilized for fault detection and classification in photovoltaic (PV) systems. They offer robustness against overfitting and are effective when handling large datasets with numerous variables ().
Support Vector Machines (SVM): SVMs are employed for classification and regression tasks, such as predicting the performance of wind turbines and PV panels. Their strength lies in finding optimal hyperplanes in high-dimensional spaces, making them well suited to complex pattern recognition ().
Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs): ANNs, particularly feedforward and recurrent networks, are applied in forecasting energy production and load demand. Their capacity to model intricate relationships between inputs and outputs makes them valuable for time-series prediction tasks ().
These algorithms are often integrated into hybrid models to enhance prediction accuracy and system reliability. For instance, combining SVMs with genetic algorithms has been shown to improve the optimization of energy storage systems in hybrid renewable setups ().
### 2.2 Deep learning approaches
Deep Learning (DL) techniques, a subset of ML, involve neural networks with multiple layers that model hierarchical data representations (). In RES, DL approaches are applied across three principal tasks.
Energy Forecasting: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are used to predict solar and wind energy generation by capturing temporal dependencies in time-series data. Studies have demonstrated that LSTMs outperform traditional ML models in forecasting accuracy (). LSTMs are also increasingly combined with chaos-theory-based methods for enhanced time-series prediction, as elaborated in Section 2.4.
Fault Detection: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are employed to analyse sensor data and detect anomalies indicative of faults in wind turbines and PV systems. Their ability to process spatial data makes them well suited to image-based and pattern-based diagnostics ().
Optimization: Autoencoders and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are explored for system optimization tasks such as enhancing energy storage efficiency and improving grid stability. These DL models can generate synthetic data to augment training datasets, yielding more robust optimization solutions ().
### 2.3 Reinforcement learning for control and optimization
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a paradigm in which agents learn to make decisions by interacting with an environment to maximize cumulative rewards (). In RES, RL is applied across three areas. For energy management, RL algorithms optimize the operation of hybrid energy systems by learning optimal control policies for energy storage and dispatch; Deep Q-Networks (DQNs), for example, have been utilized to manage battery storage systems by balancing charging and discharging cycles. For grid control, RL supports adaptive control strategies in smart grids, enabling dynamic response to fluctuating renewable energy inputs and varying load demands, thereby enhancing grid stability and reducing the need for manual intervention. For predictive maintenance, RL techniques are integrated with PdM frameworks to optimize maintenance schedules and resource allocation, minimizing downtime and operational costs. The integration of RL with supervised learning and optimization algorithms has shown promise in developing comprehensive solutions for the efficient management of RES.

### 4.2 AI/ML-based predictive maintenance frameworks
The integration of AI and ML into predictive maintenance frameworks has transformed maintenance paradigms in RES (). Leveraging real-time sensor data, historical performance records, and environmental conditions, AI/ML models predict equipment failures before they occur, enabling proactive maintenance actions (). These models use supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and deep learning to analyse complex datasets and uncover patterns indicative of potential failures. Deep learning approaches have, for instance, been applied to time-series data from wind turbines to forecast gearbox failures with greater accuracy than traditional methods, while ML algorithms have been utilized in photovoltaic systems to detect anomalies and anticipate panel degradation. The integration of IoT devices into RES further enhances predictive capacity through continuous monitoring and high-resolution data acquisition (). Combining IoT with AI/ML increases prediction precision, streamlines maintenance schedules, reduces downtime, and extends the operational lifespan of critical infrastructure ().
### 4.3 Case studies and applications
Wind energy systems: Siemens Gamesa’s Pythia platform employs big data analytics and intelligent algorithms to predict potential component damages up to 3 years in advance, conduct daily health checks across the drivetrain and structural subsystems, and optimize spare-part forecasts based on learned degradation trajectories. The platform integrates multi-sensor SCADA streams, vibration signals, and meteorological data into a centralized analytics architecture that supports fleet-wide monitoring. This system has demonstrated significant improvements in operational efficiency and cost savings in wind farms ().
Photovoltaic systems: A study conducted on a solar power plant utilized ML algorithms to analyse sensor data and predict panel failures. The implementation of predictive maintenance strategies resulted in a 30% reduction in maintenance costs and a 20% increase in energy production efficiency ().
Hybrid energy systems: In a hybrid solar–wind energy system, AI-based predictive maintenance models were developed to forecast component failures by analysing environmental and operational data. The application of these models led to a 25% decrease in unplanned maintenance events and enhanced system reliability ().

In RES, optimization typically involves coordinating variable generation (PV/wind), controllable resources (storage, flexible loads, backup units), and power electronic interfaces under uncertainty. AI/ML techniques are increasingly used to enhance forecasting, scheduling, energy management, and real-time control by learning nonlinear system dynamics and adapting decisions to changing operating conditions (; ). Importantly, optimization decisions, for example, storage cycling, converter switching, and dispatch setpoints directly influence component stress and degradation, creating an operational–maintenance coupling that motivates integrating optimization with PdM outputs (health indices, fault probabilities, and RUL estimates).

AI/ML applications in solar PV systems span fault classification, degradation monitoring, irradiance forecasting, and economic dispatch. CNNs and RF classifiers have been applied to detect shading, soiling, and cell degradation from thermal imaging and I–V curve data. LSTM-based models excel in short-term irradiance and generation forecasting, supporting day-ahead scheduling and storage dispatch optimization. Digital twin frameworks for PV arrays integrate real-time monitoring with physics-based degradation models, enabling RUL estimation and proactive maintenance scheduling.
### 6.2 Application to wind energy systems
Wind turbine condition monitoring and predictive maintenance represent the most mature domain for AI/ML in RES. SCADA-based anomaly detection using autoencoders and isolation forests has demonstrated early fault detection in gearboxes, generators, and pitch systems. Fleet-level monitoring platforms such as Siemens Gamesa’s Pythia system combine multi-sensor fusion with probabilistic health scoring for proactive maintenance planning. Offshore wind farm energy forecasting employs hybrid DL/statistical models that account for spatiotemporal dependencies across turbine arrays. Reinforcement learning has been applied to wake steering optimization in wind farms to maximize aggregate power extraction while managing structural loading.

results.title: Modeling Solar PV Adoption: A Social-Behavioral Agent-Based Framework
results.snippet:
Behavioral scientists contend that individuals, and organiza-
tions rarely make decisions solely on the basis of economic
factors. Decisions are also shaped by perceived risk, social
interactions, currency and salience of information, and other
value propositions. Social diffusion of information on con-
sumer experiences, entrance of new business models better
aligned with customers’ concerns when evaluating invest-
ments, and perceived improving economic conditions are all
factors in consumers’ decisions to adopt a new technology,
such as solar photovoltaics (PV). We describe a new con-
ceptual agent-based model, BE-Solar, that incorporates a
social and behavioral decision framework for technology
adoption decisions. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-
cluding heterogeneity and behavioral factors into an agent-
based model of the solar PV market, which is being applied
to the Southern California market.

In this paper, we describe a social and behavioral deci-
sion framework and a new conceptual agent-based model,
BE-Solar, that incorporates social and behavioral factors
into individuals’ decision models for technology adoption.
To assess the modeling approache’s viability, BE-Solar is
being applied to study the adoption of residential rooftop
solar photovolatics (PV) in Southern California.
Social-Behavioral Framework
Our design premise for modeling decision behaviors of res-
idential consumers is that the decision to purchase a PV
system is the outcome of a deliberative process undertaken
by motivated consumers. We incorporate principles from
behavioral economics and psychology into the representa-
tion of residential consumer decision behaviors. We adapt
concepts from innovation diffusion theory and marketing
to model a five-step consumer decision process: (1) recog-
nition: consumer becomes aware of PV systems or the op-
portunity to purchase or lease PV; (2) information search:
consumer is interested enough in PV to seek more infor-
mation, which results in the consumer forming a favorable
or unfavorable opinion about adopting the technology; (3)
evaluation of alternatives: consumer applies their value
proposition to comparing PV purchase options and the null
option to not adopt; (4) purchase decision: consumer
chooses to purchase or not purchase a PV system; and (5)
post-decision behavior: consumer seeks reinforcement of
their adoption decision (or reverses it) and communicates
positive (or negative) PV perceptions within their social
network.

If no conflicting or negative information is obtained during
the information search, the consumer pursues the purchase
decision by evaluating alternatives. For this evaluation, we
invoke concepts from Rogers (2005) diffusion of innova-
tion theory. Rogers postulates, and supports with empirical
evidence, five perceived attributes of innovations that af-
fect their rate of adoption: (1) relative advantage (degree
of superiority over its replacement or alternative); (2) com-
patibility (degree of consistency with existing values, past
experiences and needs; (3) complexity (degree of difficulty
to understand and/or use); (4) trialability (ability for lim-
ited testing or experience); and (5) observability (visibility
to others).  Gatignon and Robertson (1985) also include
perceived risk (expectations for economic or social loss) as
a separate innovation attribute.

Agent Social-Behavioral Model
The factors described below are either screening criteria
or quantitative measures. The screening criteria signify a
go or no-go decision based on hard constraints that the
consumer cannot affect. An example of a hard constraint is
a consumer who cannot pay for a solar PV installation
from either cash on hand or through a loan.  Each of the
screening factors results in a single outcome: screening cri-
teria result in a yes or no outcome; quantitative criteria re-
sult in a numeric quantity. A no for any screening criteria
means the decision is to not adopt solar PV. If all screening
criteria have a yes result, the other factors are computed
and the results are combined in a value function. The deci-
sion to adopt is based on a value threshold.  If the value
function is greater than the threshold, the decision is to
adopt solar PV. If the value function is less than the
threshold, the decision is to not adopt solar PV.

results.title: An ensemble-based enhanced short and medium term load forecasting using optimized missing value imputation
results.snippet:
Electricity load forecasting is integral to planning, energy management, and the energy market. Utility companies serve a massive number of customers by supplying electricity. These utility companies require a precise forecast of electricity usage. This paper presents a forecasting model for energy load based on the ensemble voting regressor method. In addition, to enhance the accuracy of forecasting, develop an imputation method for handling missing values in the user’s energy consumption data. A real-time data set is used for performance comparison with multiple imputation techniques to validate the imputation approach by generating random missing data for different missing rates of 10–30%. The proposed forecasting model is compared with other state-of-the-art methods to show its effectiveness in terms of MAPE, MAE, and RMSE. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methodology significantly improves the accuracy of the predicted load for a day and week ahead of energy consumption.

This paper offers a solution to this issue by enhancing load forecasting accuracy of electric load using a combination of ensemble voting regressor prediction models with properly counter the missing values with an efficient imputation technique. Three distinct machine learning (ML) prediction algorithms integrate with an ensembling model for a more reliable and precise prediction. A hybrid ensemble technique improves forecasting performance by utilizing the variety and complementary capabilities of these algorithms along with an efficient technique for addressing missing data. This paper conducts a comparative study of different missing value imputation techniques; chooses the best one; and applies it to different prediction models to estimate the energy load. To fill in the missing value, this paper proposes spline interpolation. By using this method, missing data will less negatively impact the forecasting process, and the load estimates will be more accurate.
In this research, three regression models, random forest (RF), extra tree (ET), and decision tree (DT), ML algorithms are ensembled which are considered to be a better method than using a single ML algorithm. The outputs of these regression models are combined using simple averaging to provide a single forecast, referred to as the ensemble voting regressor (EVR). This approach seeks to improve load forecasts’ accuracy, robustness, and reliability by combining multiple models and effectively handling missing data, facilitating more informed decisions for energy management and grid operation.

This paper presents a combined approach for load forecasting in consideration of the missing values present in the dataset. This approach is suitable for effectively predicting the electricity consumption for short-term (one day) and medium-term (one week) LF.

This study proposes a hybrid EVR prediction model that integrates the attributes of three distinct machine learning algorithms to estimate the electricity demand in smart grids for both short-term (one-hour and one-day ahead) and medium-term (one-week ahead) periods with an hour resolution. Furthermore, an imputation technique is developed to address missing values in smart meter datasets, thereby enhancing the accuracy of demand forecasts.

results.title: Modeling green energy consumption: nexus of normative beliefs and social-psychological motivations for residential solar PV adoption
results.snippet:
People's environmental consciousness and social-psychological motivations primarily drive the transition from fossil fuels to alternative energy sources. In light of this, the study's main aim is to analyze a combined approach of the “modified Norm Activation Model” (m-NAM) and the “extended Theory of Planned Behavior” (eTPB), driven by normative beliefs and social-psychological motivations, to comprehend the phenomenon of green energy consumption for residential solar electricity.
## Design/methodology/approach
To analyze this phenomenon, a multi-model analytical framework (mNAM, eTPB and “Unified mNAM-eTPB”) has been operationalized. In doing so, we thus separately examined each of the three models that were put forth: “mNAM” with subjective norms and PBC (model 1), “eTPB” with perceived policy effectiveness (model 2), and “Unified mNAM-eTPB” (model 3—the test model) using direct paths with SEM and mediation approach with PROCESS macro from the responses received from solar power users in India.
## Findings
The findings corroborate the robustness of each of the three models with underlying relationships, both directly and indirectly, in the study. Furthermore, the outcomes confirm that the “eTPB” components and the intended behaviors in the test model are partially mediated by pro-environmental attitudes and individual norms. The research thus validates that combining social-psychological cues with normative perspectives – resulting in the “Unified mNAM-eTPB” methodology – leads to a more profound understanding of people's behavior regarding home solar power use.

Advancing renewable energy literature, this study pioneers a “Unified mNAM-eTPB” framework, uniquely integrating novel cognitive factors and psychological elements, including perceived policy effectiveness. It comprehensively analyses household solar electricity adoption decisions, addressing a crucial contextual gap in the Indian context.

results.title: Hybrid feature-based neural network regression method for load profiles forecasting
results.snippet:
This study addresses the critical need for improved demand forecasting models that can accurately predict energy consumption, particularly in the context of varying geographical and climatic conditions. The work introduces a novel demand forecasting model that integrates clustering techniques and feature engineering into neural network regression, with a specific focus on incorporating correlations with air temperature. Evaluation of the model’s efficacy utilized a benchmark dataset from Tetouan, Morocco, where existing forecasting methods yielded RMSE values ranging from 6429 to 10,220 [MWh]. In contrast, the proposed approach achieved a significantly lower RMSE of 5168, indicating its superiority. Subsequent application of the model to forecast demand in Astana, Kazakhstan, as a case study, showcased its efficacy further. Comparative analysis against a baseline neural network method revealed a notable improvement, with the proposed model exhibiting a MAPE of 5.19% compared to the baseline’s 17.36%. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed approach to enhance demand forecasting accuracy, particularly across diverse geographical contexts, by leveraging climate-related inputs, the methodology also demonstrates potential for broader applications, such as flood forecasting, agricultural yield prediction, or water resource management.

Gupta and Panda [[34](/article/10.1186/s42162-025-00481-0#ref-CR34)] propose a new method to study the relationship between temperature variation and load variation using real-time data collected every thirty minutes. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is adopted to decompose load variation to find the weather sensitive portion of load and regression is applied to compare the effectiveness of using variation values and real values of load demand and temperature. results.snippet:
A Scalable Predictive Maintenance Model for
Detecting Wind Turbine Component Failures Based
on SCADA Data
Lorenzo Gigoni, Alessandro Betti
i-EM S.r.l
Livorno, Italy
lorenzo.gigoni@i-em.eu
Mauro Tucci, Emanuele Crisostomi
University of Pisa
Pisa, Italy
mauro.tucci@unipi.it
Abstract—In this work, a novel predictive maintenance system
is presented and applied to the main components of wind
turbines. The proposed model is based on machine learning and
statistical process control tools applied to SCADA (Supervisory
Control And Data Acquisition) data of critical components. The
test campaign was divided into two stages: a ﬁrst two years
long ofﬂine test, and a second one year long real-time test. The
ofﬂine test used historical faults from six wind farms located
in Italy and Romania, corresponding to a total of 150 wind
turbines and an overall installed nominal power of 283 MW.
The results demonstrate outstanding capabilities of anomaly
prediction up to 2 months before device unscheduled downtime.
Furthermore, the real-time 12-months test conﬁrms the ability
of the proposed system to detect several anomalies, therefore
allowing the operators to identify the root causes, and to schedule
maintenance actions before reaching a catastrophic stage.

In this paper a novel predictive maintenance model for WT
sub-components failures was presented, based on the integra-
tion of Machine Learning and statistical process control tools,
and applying a multivariate approach at all the processing
levels. The model is fed with SCADA tags and is composed
mainly by four processing phases: (i) an outliers removal phase
based on power curve modeling and k-means clustering, (ii)
a seasonally adjusting procedure for temperature signals, (iii)
an AANN-based residual approach to normalize tags, (iv) and
ﬁnally a residual control chart based on a novel KPI formula
to trigger components warnings. Results from a vast campaign
on 150 wind turbines demonstrate the ability of the proposed
methodology to predict failures at gearbox, generator and main
bearing levels, with lead times up to 1-2 months, and ensuring
early detection at least.
